title: Limit Order Book and Matching Engine
context:
The limit order book is the beating heart of every exchange and every market maker: a price-time-priority structure that must accept, cancel and match hundreds of thousands of orders per second while never getting the queue order wrong. Bugs here are not crashes — they are trades at wrong prices, priority violations that other members can litigate, and phantom liquidity.

This project asks you to build a working book and matching engine with the semantics an exchange specification would describe, prove them with correctness tests (including property tests), and measure throughput. The design constraints are deliberate: integer tick prices (floating point never touches matching logic), deterministic replay from an order log, and complexity targets you must actually meet.
problem:
Implement a price-time-priority limit order book and matching engine in C++17:

- **Orders**: limit and market orders on two sides, with unique ids, integer-tick prices and quantities; add, cancel-by-id and replace (price/quantity) operations.
- **Matching**: incoming marketable orders cross against the opposite side in price-time priority; partial fills supported; trades are emitted as records (maker id, taker id, price, quantity); resting quantities persist.
- **Queries**: best bid/ask, depth to N levels per side, total quantity within k ticks of the mid.
- **Correctness**: an assert-based test suite covering crossing, partial fills, cancels (including cancel-after-fill), FIFO within a price level, and property tests (randomised operation sequences maintain invariants: no crossed book, no negative quantities, every id either live or consumed exactly once).
- **Performance**: a throughput benchmark driving at least 1M mixed operations; report ops/sec and the breakdown (add/cancel/match); deterministic replay from a logged operation sequence must reproduce identical final book state and trades.
requirements: Price-time priority exactly: FIFO within each price level, best price first; market orders execute immediately against the book (or are rejected if the book is empty — the choice documented).
Integer ticks for all prices in matching logic (`std::int64_t`); any conversion to/from decimal lives at the API edge and is documented (tick size, rounding).
Cancel/replace is O(1) amortised via an order-id to location map plus level structures; add is O(log P) worst case (P = number of price levels) with the chosen structure documented.
Depth queries return per-level or cumulative quantities (pick and document); best bid/ask in O(1).
Trades and fills emitted in matching order with maker/taker attribution; the trade log can be replayed to rebuild the exact final book.
Property tests with a seeded RNG over at least 100k random operations asserting the invariants (no crossing, no negative qty, id-liveness consistency).

Throughput benchmark with a mixed workload (e.g. 60% add, 25% cancel, 15% marketable) reporting ops/sec, plus a notes section on the measured bottleneck and one concrete optimisation attempt with before/after numbers.

designGuidance.md: The classic trade-off: `std::map<Price, Level, std::greater<>>` for bids gives ordered iteration and O(log P) insertion with zero tuning, while `std::unordered_map<Price, Level>` plus a cached best-price pointer gives O(1) inserts and queries but needs careful maintenance on level exhaustion. Either is defensible — write down which you chose, why, and what the worst case is. Do not benchmark your way to a design before you can state the complexity argument.

designGuidance.title: Floating point and prices do not mix
designGuidance.md: `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3` is a book corruption waiting to happen: two 'equal' prices that compare unequal break FIFO grouping and matching. Represent prices as integer ticks end-to-end (`int64_t`), convert at the boundary, and never let a `double` reach the matching code.

rows: O(log P) or O(1) by design
ordered map vs hash + cached best
cached pointers updated on level change
walk opposite side, pop filled quantities

designGuidance.caption: One workable skeleton — justify any deviation

items: After any operation: best_bid < best_ask (no crossed book) — assert at operation boundaries, not inside matching.
Every order id is in exactly one state: live in the book, fully filled, or cancelled — never two, never zero-without-history.
Level totals equal the sum of their orders (maintain incrementally; assert in tests, not in the hot path).
Replay: the same operation log produces an identical trade sequence and final book — this is your regression net for any structural refactor.

designGuidance.title: Priority violations get litigated
designGuidance.md: Exchanges publish their matching priority rules precisely because members audit them. If your engine ever matches a later-arriving order at a price level ahead of an earlier one at the same price, that is not a style issue — it is the kind of bug that becomes an arbitration case. Test FIFO explicitly with same-price orders arriving in sequence.

# Limit order book build sketch.
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(limit_order_book CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
enable_testing()

add_library(lob STATIC
  src/lob/book.cpp
  # TODO(project): src/lob/matching.cpp
)
target_include_directories(lob PUBLIC ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)
target_compile_options(lob PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra)

# TODO(project): register test executables with add_test once written.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Matching semantics correctness: price-time priority, partial fills, cancels, market orders
Data-structure design meets stated complexity targets; integer-tick discipline
Test suite: scenarios, property tests with invariants, replay determinism
Throughput benchmark methodology and bottleneck analysis with before/after
Documentation: semantics spec, design decisions, build/run instructions

documentationRequirements: README.md: order-lifecycle semantics spec (add/cancel/replace/match), order-state table, build and run instructions.
The complexity table from design guidance, updated to the structures you actually chose.
Benchmark section: workload mix, hardware, ops/sec, bottleneck notes and optimisation result.
The invariants list asserted by tests, so reviewers know what the suite guarantees.
extensionChallenges: Add stop orders (trigger on the last trade price crossing a threshold) and decide their interaction with priority.
Implement a pooled node allocator for level FIFOs and measure allocation-count and throughput changes.
Add self-trade prevention with tests for the three standard policies (cancel-newest, cancel-oldest, cancel-both).
